title: Where food comes from: food from plants and food from animals

summary.text: A mango tree never eats, yet the tree grows big and makes mangoes. Plants make their own food from sunlight, air and water. Animals, including us, cannot do that, so we eat plants and other animals. Some of our food comes from plants, like rice, coconut and palak. Some comes from animals, like milk, eggs and honey. In this unit you make pretend flower nectar from sugar water and find out how bees turn nectar into thick honey.
summary.art: A mango tree in sunshine on one side, and a child eating idli with a cup of milk and a spoon of honey on the other, with small drawings of a cow, a hen and a bee.

intro.hook: Hold a spoon of honey and tip it slowly. The honey creeps off the spoon. Now tip a spoon of water. The water runs off at once. Bees make honey from a thin, watery juice inside flowers. How do they make it so thick?
intro.text: Every food we eat comes from somewhere. Most of it comes from plants or from animals. In this unit you sort your lunch into food from plants and food from animals. You find out that plants make their own food, and animals must eat. Then you test what happens to thin sugar water under a fan, the way bees make honey.
intro.art: A child tipping two steel spoons side by side: honey creeping off one in a slow golden ribbon, water splashing off the other.

outcomes: By the end I can sort foods into food from plants and food from animals, and give two examples of each.
By the end I can say that plants make their own food from sunlight, air and water, and that animals, including us, eat plants or other animals.
By the end I can say how bees make honey from flower nectar, using what I saw in my sugar water test.
By the end I can say where milk, eggs and honey come from, and what the animals who make them eat.
By the end I can make a guess, say why, watch carefully and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: Food is what a living being takes in to grow, move and stay alive.
terms.example: Rice, a banana and a glass of milk are all food.
terms.art: A steel plate with rice, a banana and a glass of milk.

terms.meaning: Some of our food is a part of a plant: a seed, a fruit, a leaf, a root or a stem.
terms.example: Rice is a seed. A mango is a fruit. Palak is a leaf. A carrot is a root.
terms.art: Rice grains, a mango, a palak leaf and a carrot in a row, each with a small drawing of the plant they came from.

terms.meaning: Some of our food comes from animals. Animals make milk, eggs and honey, and some people also eat fish and meat.
terms.example: A cow makes milk. A hen lays eggs. Honey bees make honey.
terms.art: A cow with a pot of milk, a hen with an egg, and a bee on a honeycomb.

terms.meaning: Nectar is a thin, sweet juice that flowers make inside them. Bees and butterflies drink nectar.
terms.example: A bee pushes her head into a flower to drink the nectar.
terms.art: A honey bee with her head inside a pink flower, and a tiny shining drop of nectar.

terms.meaning: When water evaporates, it goes into the air as tiny bits too small to see.
terms.example: Wet clothes on a line dry because the water evaporates into the air.
terms.art: Clothes drying on a balcony line, with faint wavy lines rising from them into the air.

explanations.definition: Green plants make food in their leaves, from sunlight, air and water.
explanations.description: A plant does not eat. Roots drink water, and leaves take in air. Sunlight gives the leaves the energy to make sugar. That sugar is the plant's food.
examples: A mango tree makes all the food in every mango from sunlight, air and water.
Sugarcane stores sweet juice in the stem. The plant made that sugar in the leaves.
In the 1930s, Janaki Ammal, a plant scientist from Kerala, helped breed sweeter sugarcane in Coimbatore.
explanations.context: This card is about how plants get their food.
explanations.art: A green leaf in sunlight, with a blue arrow of water coming up from the roots and a small arrow of air going into the leaf.

explanations.definition: Animals cannot make food from sunlight. So every animal eats plants, or eats other animals, or both.
explanations.description: Humans are animals too. A cow eats grass. A hen pecks grain and insects. A crow eats almost anything. You eat rice, dal, vegetables, and maybe milk, eggs or fish.
examples: A goat eats leaves. A tiger eats deer. A crow eats seeds, insects and leftovers.
A baby drinks milk from their mother before they can eat anything else.
A child in Kolkata may eat rice and fish. A child in Madurai may eat idli and sambar.
explanations.context: This card is about why animals, including people, must eat.
explanations.art: A cow eating grass, a hen pecking grain, a crow with a seed, and a child eating rice, all in one row.

explanations.definition: Much of our food is a part of a plant: seeds, fruits, leaves, roots, stems and even flowers.
explanations.description: Rice, wheat, ragi and dal are seeds. Mangoes, bananas and tomatoes are fruits. Palak and curry leaves are leaves. Carrots are roots. Banana flower is a flower.
examples: A dosa is made from rice and urad dal. Both are seeds.
Coconut is the fruit of the coconut palm.
In the 1940s, Kamala Sohonie, the first Indian woman to earn a PhD in science, studied neera. Neera is the sweet sap of palm trees.
explanations.context: This card is about the parts of plants that we eat.
explanations.art: A banana leaf thali with rice, sambar, a banana, palak and a coconut chutney, each with a small leaf mark.

explanations.definition: Animals give us milk, eggs and honey. Some people also eat fish and meat.
explanations.description: A cow, buffalo or goat makes milk for her calf or kid. A hen lays eggs. Honey bees make honey to feed their hive. Curd, ghee and paneer are all made from milk. Many families eat no meat, and some eat no eggs or honey either.
examples: In Rajasthan and Kutch, some families drink camel milk.
Most eggs from a shop cannot hatch. There was no rooster, so no chick began inside.
A cow makes milk from the grass she eats. So the milk began as a plant.
explanations.context: This card is about food that comes from animals.
explanations.art: A buffalo with her calf, a hen sitting near an egg, and a honeycomb dripping honey.

explanations.definition: Honey bees drink flower nectar, carry it home, and dry it into thick honey.
explanations.description: A worker bee sucks up nectar and carries the nectar home in her body. At the hive, the bees mix it with juices from their own bodies. They spread it in the wax cells and fan their wings over it. The moving air makes water evaporate. When the honey is thick, they close the cell with wax.
examples: All the honey-making bees in a hive are female. The male bees make no honey.
One worker bee makes less than one teaspoon of honey in her whole life.
In Kerala, people also collect cheruthen, honey from tiny bees who do not sting.
explanations.context: This card is about the sugar water test, where a drop under the fan turned thick and sticky.
explanations.art: Bees on a honeycomb fanning their wings over open cells of honey, with soft wavy lines of moving air.

explanations.description: Bees choose which flowers to visit, and they remember where the best ones are. A honey bee can tell her sisters where flowers are by dancing on the comb. Flowers make nectar and bright colours, and bees carry their pollen. Some scientists say this is all instinct, not choosing.
examples: Karl von Frisch, an Austrian scientist, found that honey bees dance to show the way to flowers.
A bee visits the same kind of flower again and again on one trip.
Flowers that bees visit grow fruits and seeds.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study bee behaviour
perspectives.explanation: Bees learn, remember, decide and tell each other where food is. Flowers sense and respond too. Both are minds at work.
Bees and flowers follow instincts built over a very long time. They prefer words like 'behaviour' and 'response' to 'choose'.

explanations.context: This card is about whether bees and flowers make choices.
explanations.art: A honey bee dancing in a figure of eight on a honeycomb, with other bees gathered round her.

agreed.text: Green plants make their own food from sunlight, air and water.
agreed.evidence: A plant in a dark cupboard goes pale and weak. A plant in light grows, though nobody feeds the plant.

agreed.text: Every animal, including people, gets food by eating plants, other animals, or both.
agreed.evidence: Watch any animal for a while: a crow, an ant, a cow, a cat. Each one is looking for food or eating.

agreed.text: Honey bees make honey from flower nectar.
agreed.evidence: Beekeepers see bees going into flowers and coming home. When there are few flowers, the bees make little honey.

challenging.claim: Honey falls from the air like dew, and bees only gather it.
challenging.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 2,350 years ago
challenging.for: Bees sometimes gather sweet drops from leaves, and the drops seem to appear from nowhere.
challenging.against: Bees drink nectar from flowers and dry it in the hive. The sweet drops on leaves are mostly made by tiny insects sucking the plant.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where honey comes from.

challenging.claim: Every food comes from a plant or an animal.
challenging.for: Almost everything on our plate does come from a plant or an animal.
challenging.against: Salt comes from sea water or from the ground. Water comes from rain, rivers and wells. Mushrooms are fungi, which are neither plants nor animals.
challenging.context: This card is about foods that are neither plant nor animal.

challenging.for: We buy milk in a packet or from a milk booth.
challenging.against: The shop only sells the milk. A cow, a buffalo or a goat made the milk, from the plants she ate.
challenging.context: This card is about where milk really comes from.

big_questions.q: Honey is made by bees from flower nectar. Is honey food from a plant, food from an animal, or both?
big_questions.hint: Think about who made the nectar, and who made it thick.

big_questions.q: A cow makes milk from the grass she eats. Is the milk made of grass?
big_questions.hint: Think about what goes into the cow, and what comes out.

big_questions.q: Plants make their own food. If you could make food from sunlight, how would your day be different?
big_questions.hint: Think about meals, cooking and going to the shop.

big_questions.q: Bees make honey for their own hive. When we take honey, who should it belong to?
big_questions.hint: Think about the bees, the flowers and the beekeeper.

story.title: The Hum Under the Water Tank
story.note: Divya, her Ajji (grandmother) and her Appa (father) are made up. The bee facts are true: rock bees build one large open comb, often under ledges and water tanks in Indian cities. They sting if disturbed, and they move to a new place after some months.
text: Divya lived on the fourth floor of a tall building in Bengaluru. She was six. One morning she heard a soft, steady hum outside her window.
Under the water tank of the next building hung a huge brown shape. The shape was as big as a door, and the shape was moving.
'Ajji!' she called. Ajji, her grandmother, came slowly with her glasses.
'Rock bees,' said Ajji. 'They have built a honeycomb. Thousands of bees are sitting on the comb, keeping it safe.'
Appa, her father, came to look. 'We must call someone to burn it,' he said. 'Bees sting.'
'Rock bees sting if you disturb them,' said Ajji. 'So we will not disturb them. We will watch from inside, with the window shut. Rock bees move on after some months.'
So every day, Divya watched through the glass. Bees flew away from the comb in a stream. Other bees flew back.
'Where do they go?' she asked.

'To the flowers,' said Ajji. 'Look at the drumstick tree in the park, and the yellow flowers on the gulmohar road. Inside each flower is a drop of sweet juice called nectar. A bee drinks the nectar and carries the nectar home inside her.'
'Is it honey already?' asked Divya.

'Not yet. Nectar is thin and watery. The bees spread it in little wax rooms in the comb. Then they fan their wings over it, hour after hour. The moving air dries it. Slowly it turns thick. Then it is honey.'
Appa put down his phone. 'I did not know that,' he said. 'I thought honey just came in a bottle.'
Divya laughed. 'Appa, the bottle cannot make honey. Only bees can.'
That night at dinner, Divya looked at her plate. There were dosas, coconut chutney and a small cup of curd.
'Ajji, did bees make my dosa?'
'No,' said Ajji. 'A dosa is rice and urad dal. Both are seeds from plants. The coconut grew on a coconut palm.'
'And the curd?'
'The curd was milk. A cow made the milk from the grass she ate.'
Divya put a leaf drawing next to the dosa and the chutney. She put a cow drawing next to the curd. 'Food from plants, and food from animals,' she said.
'And honey?' asked Appa.
Divya thought for a long time. 'Honey is both,' she said. 'The flower made the nectar. The bees made the nectar into honey.'
Ajji smiled. 'And the flower got something back. When a bee drinks, yellow pollen sticks to her. She carries the pollen to the next flower, and that helps the flowers make seeds.'
The weeks went by. The rains came. One morning the hum was gone. The rock bees had flown away, all together, to a new home somewhere else.
Only the empty comb was left, pale and full of little holes.
Divya pressed her nose to the window. 'Thank you for not burning them, Appa,' she said.
'Thank Ajji,' said Appa. 'She taught me to look first.'
Divya tried it at home the next day. She made sugar water, thin like nectar. She put a little on a plate under the fan. By morning it was thick and sticky, just like honey.
'The fan was my bee,' she said.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Divya sorts her dinner into food from plants and food from animals, and then sees that honey belongs to both. A flower made the nectar, and the bees dried it into honey.
ask: Where did the bees fly to every day, and why?
How do bees make thin nectar into thick honey?
Why did Divya say honey is both?
art: A girl at a fourth-floor window in Bengaluru, looking at a huge brown honeycomb hanging under a water tank on the next building.
Bees flying in a stream from the comb towards yellow flowers and a drumstick tree in a park below.
A grandmother explaining to a father at a window, while the girl watches the bees through the glass.
A dinner plate with dosas, coconut chutney and curd, and a child's small drawings of a leaf and a cow beside them.
An empty pale honeycomb under the water tank after the rains, with the girl's face pressed to the window.

games.title: Leaf Plate, Cow Plate: a food sorting game
games.context: This is a card game about where food comes from. Each card names a food. Players put the card on the leaf plate for food from plants, or the cow plate for food from animals. A few tricky cards are both, or neither.

rules: Before you play, your child draws the food on each card under the word, so a child who cannot read can play. The reader reads out each word.
Put the four plate labels on the floor. Put the leaf plate and the cow plate in front, and Both and Neither at the side.
Mix the cards and put them in a pile, words up.
On your turn, take the top card and say the food. Put the card on the plate where you think the card belongs.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. If you were right, make a mark by your name on a sheet of paper. If not, move the card to the right plate.
When the pile is empty, count your marks. The most marks wins. If two players have the same, they both win. Playing alone, try to beat your marks from last time.

flow.do: 1. Read each card to your child. 2. Your child draws the food on each card. 3. Lay out the four plate labels.
flow.say: Each card is a food. Draw the food on the card. Then we sort them.
flow.kid: Draw a little picture of each food.

flow.do: 1. Take turns with the cards. 2. Read the back of each card aloud. 3. Stop at the tricky cards and talk about them.
flow.say: Where does honey go? Who made the nectar, and who made the honey?
flow.kid: Take a card. Leaf plate or cow plate? Say why.

ask.q: Why does curd go on the cow plate, when curd does not look like a cow?
good: Curd is made from milk.
A cow made the milk.

flow.parent: The tricky cards are the point. Let your child argue for a plate before you read the back.

flow.do: Count the cards on each plate together. Count each player's marks. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Which plate has the most cards? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count the cards on each plate. Which has the most? Count your marks.

check.q: Which plate does a banana go on?
check.why: A banana is the fruit of the banana plant. So a banana is food from a plant.

setup.caption: 1. Draw a food on each card.

setup.art: Two steel plates on the floor, one with a leaf drawn on paper beside it and one with a cow, with cards being placed on each, and two small paper squares marked Both and Neither.
setup.caption: 2. Put each card on the leaf plate, the cow plate, Both or Neither.

games.title: Who Made My Food? a memory game
games.context: This is a memory game. Half the cards show a food, and half show the plant or animal who made that food. Players turn over two cards at a time to find a food and their maker.

rules: Before you play, draw on each card: the food, or the plant or animal.
Mix the cards and lay them face down in rows of five.
On your turn, turn over two cards. If one is a food and the other is the plant or animal who made that food, keep both. Then take another turn.
If they do not match, turn them face down again. The next player has a turn.
When all the cards are matched, the player with the most pairs wins. If two players have the same, they both win.

flow.do: 1. Read each card to your child. 2. Draw the pictures together. 3. Lay the cards face down in four rows of five.
flow.say: Each food has a maker. Let's draw them all, then hide them.
flow.kid: Draw each card. Then turn them face down.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over two cards. 2. Each time someone finds a pair, say the pair out loud.
flow.say: Honey and honey bees! The bees made the honey from flower nectar.
flow.kid: Turn two cards. Is it a food and their maker?

ask.q: You found milk and a cow. What does the cow eat to make the milk?
good: Grass.
Grass and leaves and other plants.

flow.do: Count the pairs. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Who found the most pairs? Now one question.
flow.kid: Count your pairs.

check.q: Which of these makers is a plant?
check.why: Sugarcane is a plant. The sweet juice in the stem becomes jaggery. A hen and honey bees are animals.

setup.caption: 1. Lay the cards face down. Turn over two at a time.

setup.art: A child holding up a matched pair: a card with a coconut and a card with a coconut palm.
setup.caption: 2. A food and their maker make a pair.

experiments.title: Nectar to Honey: what turns thin sugar water thick?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make pretend flower nectar from sugar water. You put a drop under a fan and cover another drop with a katori. The next morning you tilt both plates and see which one runs.
experiments.question: We leave thin sugar water out overnight, one drop under a fan and one drop covered. Which one will turn thick, like honey?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Tomorrow, will the drop under the fan be runny like water, or thick like honey? What about the covered drop? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both drops are the same sugar water, the same size, on the same kind of plate, in the same room. Only one thing is different: one drop is open to the moving air, and one is covered by a katori.
results_table: How the drop looks and feels
What happens when we tilt the plate

materials.item: a small cup or katori, to mix in
two steel plates, or two steel lids
a katori or small bowl to cover one drop
a ceiling fan or table fan, or a sunny window
a little honey, if your family eats honey, to compare

schedule.what: Make sugar water. Feel how runny it is. Guess. Put one drop under the fan, and cover one drop with a katori.
In the evening, peep at both drops without touching them.
Touch both drops. Tilt both plates. Say what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Draw the two plates after you tilted them. Show which drop ran and which one stayed.

flow.do: 1. Put 4 spoons of water in a cup. 2. Your child adds 1 spoon of sugar. 3. Stir until the water is clear again. 4. Your child tastes a drop on a clean finger.
flow.say: This is pretend nectar. Flower nectar is thin and sweet like this. Taste it. Is it runny like water, or thick like honey?
flow.kid: Stir the sugar into the water. Taste one drop. Is it thin or thick?

ask.q: How is this sugar water like honey? How is it different?
good: Both are sweet.
The sugar water is runny. Honey is thick.

flow.parent: If you have honey, let your child tip a spoon of honey too, and see how slowly it moves.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, and to say why. Write the guess down, or draw it.
flow.say: One drop will stay under the fan all night. One drop will hide under a katori. Which one will turn thick? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which drop will turn thick? Why?

good: The fan one, because the fan will dry it.
Both will stay the same, because nothing is added.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good guess. Do not say which is right. The test will show.

flow.do: 1. Put a few drops of sugar water on each plate. 2. Spread each drop with the back of the spoon, to the size of a coin. 3. Cover one drop with an upside-down katori. 4. Put both plates on a high table under the fan.
flow.say: Both drops are the same. Only one has a cover. Now we leave them all night.
flow.kid: Put a drop on each plate. Cover one drop with a katori.
flow.wait: Leave both plates under the fan until the evening.
flow.parent: Sugar brings ants. If ants visit your home, stand each plate on an upside-down bowl inside a tray with a little water. Ants do not cross the water.

flow.do: In the evening, look at both drops together. Do not touch them yet.
flow.say: Look at the two drops. Has either one changed? Is one smaller?
flow.kid: Look at both drops. Has one changed?
flow.wait: Leave both plates under the fan overnight.

flow.do: 1. Lift the katori. 2. Your child touches each drop with a clean fingertip. 3. Tilt each plate slowly, and watch each drop. 4. Put a drop of honey on a plate and tilt that too.
flow.say: Touch each drop. Now tilt the plates slowly. Which drop runs? Which one stays?
flow.kid: Touch each drop. Tilt each plate. Which drop runs?

ask.q: What happened to the drop under the fan? What happened to the covered drop?
good: The fan drop went thick and sticky. It hardly moved.
The covered drop was still wet and ran down the plate.

flow.parent: The open drop is usually thick, sticky and smaller. It may even dry into a hard, shiny crust. The covered drop stays runny, and you may see tiny water drops inside the katori. In very damp weather, leave the plates one more day.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why. 2. Then tell them how bees make honey.
flow.say: The moving air took water out of the open drop. The water evaporated. Bees fan their wings over nectar in the same way, until the nectar turns thick. That is honey.
flow.kid: The fan dried the open drop. Bees fan nectar with their wings. Then nectar turns into honey.

ask.q: Why did the covered drop stay runny?
good: The katori kept the moving air away.
The water could not go off into the room.

check.q: The open drop turned thick, and the covered drop stayed runny. Why?
options: Moving air made the water evaporate from the open drop
The katori made the drop cold
check.why: Nothing was added to either drop. Moving air carried water away from the open drop, so less water was left with the sugar. Under the katori, the water could not get away.

activities.title: Leaf Plate, Cow Plate: sort your lunch
activities.context: In this activity you sort the foods from your kitchen or your lunch. Food from plants goes on one plate, and food from animals goes on the other.

materials.item: two steel plates, with a leaf drawn on paper beside one and a cow beside the other
small bits of 8 to 10 foods from the kitchen: a few grains of rice, some dal, a banana, a coconut piece, a curry leaf, a spoon of curd, a little ghee, salt, and an egg if your family eats eggs
a small katori for foods that fit neither plate

schedule.what: Set out small bits of kitchen foods. Sort them onto the leaf plate and the cow plate. Talk about the tricky ones.

activities.record: Draw your two plates and the foods on each.

flow.do: 1. Draw a leaf and a cow on two pieces of paper. 2. Put one beside each plate. 3. Set out the foods.
flow.say: This is the leaf plate, for food from plants. This is the cow plate, for food from animals.
flow.kid: This is the leaf plate. This is the cow plate.

ask.q: What do you notice about the foods on the table?
good: Some are seeds, like rice.
Some are white and runny, like curd.

flow.do: Your child picks up each food, says what it is, and puts it on a plate. Ask why each time.
flow.say: Where does this go? Who made this food, a plant or an animal?
flow.kid: Pick a food. Put it on the leaf plate or the cow plate. Say why.

good: The cow plate, because ghee is made from milk.
Where does salt go?
Is an egg from a plant or an animal?

flow.parent: Salt goes in the small katori. Salt comes from sea water or the ground, and no plant or animal made salt. Don't explain the others yet. Let your child argue.

flow.do: Count the foods on each plate together.
flow.say: Which plate has more food on it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count the foods on each plate. Which has more?

ask.q: Why do you think the leaf plate has more?
good: We eat lots of plants.
Rice and dal and vegetables are all plants.

flow.parent: In most Indian kitchens, the leaf plate wins easily. Even in families who eat fish or meat, most of a meal is rice, wheat, dal and vegetables.

setup.art: Two steel plates on a kitchen floor, one beside a paper with a leaf drawn on it and one beside a paper with a cow, and small bits of food in a line in front.
setup.caption: 1. Make a leaf plate and a cow plate.

setup.art: A child putting a banana on the leaf plate, with rice and a curry leaf already there, and a spoon of curd on the cow plate.
setup.caption: 2. Sort each food onto a plate. Say why.

activities.title: The Feely Bag: guess the food by touch
activities.context: In this activity you put your hand in a cloth bag and feel a food you cannot see. You guess the food, then say if it came from a plant or an animal.

materials.item: a cloth bag, or a pillow cover
7 whole foods to feel: a potato, an onion, a lemon, a banana, a peanut in the shell, a piece of coconut, and one animal food, a boiled egg in the shell or a piece of paneer in a small bag

schedule.what: Put whole foods in a bag. Feel each one, guess it, and say if it came from a plant or an animal.

activities.record: Draw the food that was hardest to guess.

flow.do: Without your child seeing, put the foods in the bag.
flow.say: There are some foods in this bag. You can only use your hands. No peeping!
flow.kid: Put your hand in the bag. No peeping!

flow.do: 1. Your child feels one food and describes the food out loud. 2. They guess. 3. They take it out to check. 4. They say plant or animal.
flow.say: Is it smooth or rough? Hard or soft? What do you think it is? Did a plant or an animal make this food?
flow.kid: Feel one food. Is it smooth or rough? Guess. Then take it out.

ask.q: How did you know it was a peanut?
good: It was bumpy and light.
It rattled when I shook it.

flow.do: Look at all the foods together.
flow.say: How many came from plants? How many came from animals?
flow.kid: Count the plant foods. Count the animal foods.

ask.q: Which part of a plant is the potato, and which part is the peanut?
good: The potato grows under the soil.
The peanut is a seed.

flow.parent: A potato is a fat stem that grows under the soil. A peanut is a seed, and peanut pods grow under the soil too. An onion is made of thick leaves.

setup.art: A cloth bag on a floor mat, with a child's hand inside it and a parent watching.
setup.caption: 1. Feel a food in the bag. No peeping.

setup.art: A potato, an onion, a lemon, a banana, a peanut in the shell and a coconut piece in a row on a mat.
setup.caption: 2. Take each food out. Plant or animal?

activities.title: The Ants' Menu: what do ants carry home?
activities.context: In this activity you put tiny bits of different foods near where ants walk. Then you watch which foods the ants find and carry away. Ants eat food from plants and from animals, like many people do.

materials.item: a piece of paper or a small steel lid
tiny bits of 4 foods: a few grains of sugar, a crumb of chapati or idli, a tiny bit of boiled egg white or paneer, and a grain of raw rice

schedule.what: Put four tiny food bits near an ant trail. Watch for 5 minutes, then check again after half an hour.

activities.record: Draw the four foods and draw ants next to the ones they visited.

flow.do: 1. Find where ants walk: the kitchen floor, a window ledge, or near the dustbin. 2. Put the paper there. 3. Put the four bits in a row, a finger apart.
flow.say: Which food do you think the ants will like best? Why?
flow.kid: Put four foods near the ants. Which one will ants like?

good: Sugar, because ants like sweet things.
The egg, because ants eat insects.

flow.do: Watch together for 5 minutes. Count the ants at each food.
flow.say: Look closely. Which food has the most ants?
flow.kid: Watch. Count the ants at each food.
flow.wait: Leave the paper for half an hour, then look again.

flow.do: Look again after half an hour. Then clean up.
flow.say: Which foods did the ants find? Did they carry any away?
flow.kid: Look again. Which foods did the ants take?

ask.q: Do ants eat food from plants, from animals, or both?
good: Both. They went to the sugar and the egg.

flow.parent: Many kinds of ants live in Indian homes, and they like different foods. Sugar is usually found first. If no ants come in an hour, try again near the kitchen sink on another day.

setup.art: A small paper on a kitchen floor near an ant trail, with four tiny food bits in a row: sugar, a chapati crumb, a bit of egg white and a rice grain.
setup.caption: 1. Put four tiny food bits near the ants.

setup.art: Close-up of small black ants gathered round the sugar grains and a few carrying a crumb away.
setup.caption: 2. Watch which foods the ants visit.

projects.title: My Food Week: a leaf and cow diary
projects.context: In this one-week project you draw what you eat each day. You put a green dot next to food from plants and a red dot next to food from animals. At the end you count the dots.

materials.item: a sheet of paper folded into 7 boxes, one for each day
a green crayon and a red crayon

schedule.what: Fold the paper into 7 boxes. Draw today's lunch in the first box. Add green and red dots.
Draw today's lunch. Add the dots.
Draw today's lunch. Add the dots.
Draw today's lunch. Add the dots.
Draw today's lunch. Add the dots.
Draw today's lunch. Add the dots.
Draw today's lunch. Count all the green dots and all the red dots. Talk about what you found.

projects.record: Keep the food week sheet, with the number of green dots and red dots written at the bottom.

flow.do: 1. Fold a sheet into 7 boxes. 2. Write a day in each box. 3. Your child draws today's lunch in the first box. 4. Put a green dot by each food from a plant and a red dot by each food from an animal.
flow.say: Draw your lunch. Then a green dot for each plant food and a red dot for each animal food.
flow.kid: Draw your lunch. Green dot for plants. Red dot for animals.
flow.wait: Do the same every day for six more days.

flow.do: Each day, your child draws lunch and adds the dots. Talk about one food each day.
flow.say: Look at today's lunch. Pick one food. Did a plant make this food, or an animal?
flow.kid: Draw today's lunch. Add the dots.

ask.q: Suppose lunch is sambar with dal, tomato and drumstick. Which dot does each one get?
good: All green. They are all from plants.

flow.parent: One food can get two dots. Curd rice gets a green dot for the rice and a red dot for the curd.

flow.do: 1. On day 7, count all the green dots. 2. Count all the red dots. 3. Write both numbers at the bottom.
flow.say: Which colour has more dots? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count the green dots. Count the red dots. Which has more?

ask.q: Why do you think there are more green dots?
good: We eat lots of rice and vegetables.
Most of our food is from plants.

flow.parent: Every family is different. A family who eats fish every day will have more red dots. The point is to look closely at what is on the plate.

setup.caption: 1. Draw lunch each day. Add green and red dots.

setup.art: The full sheet on day 7, with a child counting the green dots with a finger.
setup.caption: 2. On day 7, count the dots.

challenges.title: Be a Bee: which tongue carries the most nectar?
challenges.context: This is a making and testing challenge. You try different tools as a pretend bee's tongue. You find out which one carries the most sugar water from a cup to a bottle cap.
challenges.problem: A bee must carry nectar home from many flowers. Which of five tools carries the most sugar water from a cup to a bottle cap in 10 dips?
constraints: Dip, carry, and tap or squeeze the water into the cap each time. No pouring.
materials: a cup of sugar water, the pretend nectar from the experiment
general: A spoon, because a spoon can scoop.
A straw, with a finger over the top to hold the water in.
A strip of cloth, which soaks up the water.
creative: A paintbrush, whose hairs hold water between them, like a real honey bee's hairy tongue.
A fold of paper shaped like a little cup.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own bee tongue from things at home. Give your tool 10 dips. Did your tool beat the best tool?

flow.do: Read the challenge to your child. Show the cup of sugar water, the five bottle caps and the five tools.
flow.say: You are a bee. This cup is a flower full of nectar. These caps are your hives. Which tool will carry the most?
flow.kid: You are a bee. Which tool carries the most nectar home?

ask.q: Which tool do you think will carry the most? Why?
good: The spoon, because the spoon is the biggest.
The cloth, because cloth soaks up water.

flow.do: 1. Your child gives each tool 10 dips into the cup and taps or squeezes each one into its own cap. 2. Line up the caps.
flow.say: Dip, carry, drip. Ten times. Count with me.
flow.kid: Dip, carry, drip. Do it ten times with each tool.

flow.do: Look at the five caps together. Which cap is the fullest?
flow.say: Which cap has the most nectar? Which tool did that?
flow.kid: Which cap is the fullest?

ask.q: Why did that tool carry the most?
good: It held lots of drops between the hairs.
It was big.

flow.parent: Results differ with the tools you have. The spoon often carries the most, and the paintbrush often beats the straw and the cotton bud.

flow.do: Tell your child about a real bee's tongue.
flow.say: A real honey bee has a long, hairy tongue. Nectar sticks between the hairs, like water on your paintbrush. Then she sucks the nectar up.
flow.kid: A real bee's tongue is hairy. Nectar sticks to the hairs.

check.q: How does a honey bee's tongue pick up nectar?
options: Nectar sticks between the tiny hairs on her tongue
She scoops nectar with her legs
She waits for rain to wash nectar into the hive
check.why: A honey bee's tongue is covered in tiny hairs. Nectar clings between the hairs, like water on a paintbrush, and she draws the nectar into her mouth.

setup.caption: 1. One cup of nectar, five caps, five tools.

setup.art: A child dipping a small paintbrush in the cup and dripping it into a bottle cap.

worksheets.title: Food from Plants, Food from Animals (core)

items.p: Sort these foods. Which came from a plant, and which came from an animal?
items.why: Rice, bananas and palak are parts of plants. Milk and eggs are made by animals, and curd is made from milk.

items.p: Draw a line from each food to the plant or animal who made that food.
items.why: Bees make honey from nectar. A cow makes milk. A hen lays eggs. A coconut grows on a coconut palm.
items.art: Four foods on the left and four makers on the right, mixed up: honey, milk, an egg, a coconut, and a hen, a coconut palm, bees, a cow.

items.p: Which one of these did a plant make?
items.why: A mango is the fruit of the mango tree. Eggs and milk are made by animals.

items.p: Draw your two plates from the sugar water test, the morning after. Show which drop ran when you tilted the plate.
items.a: The open drop thick and still. The covered drop running down the plate.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the open drop staying put and the covered drop running in a line.
items.art: An empty box with two plate outlines.

items.p: Green plants make their own food, using sunlight, air and water.
items.why: True. Leaves use the energy in sunlight to make sugar from air and water. The sugar is the plant's food.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the drop under the fan turn thick?
items.a: The moving air made the water evaporate. Less water was left, so the sugar water turned thick.
items.why: A strong answer says the water went into the air, and uses what the child saw: the open drop got smaller and stickier.

items.p: Kavya, aged 7, and her brother Arun, aged 5, live in Chennai. They are eating honey on dosa.

views.says: Honey is food from an animal, because bees make honey.
Honey is food from a plant, because honey comes from flowers.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other one has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then sees the other side. The flower made the nectar, and the bees dried the nectar into honey. So both are right.
items.why: Honey needs both a plant and an animal. Some foods do not fit only one group.

items.p: Three of these grew on a plant. Which one did not?
items.why: An idli is made from rice and urad dal, which are seeds. A coconut and a tomato are fruits. A hen laid the egg.

items.p: Lalitha's lunch is rice, sambar, curd, a banana and a glass of buttermilk. How many of these came from an animal?
items.why: Curd and buttermilk are both made from milk, so 2 came from an animal. Rice, sambar and the banana came from plants.

items.p: Here is the journey of honey. Write or say what is in each box: flower, bee, honeycomb, honey jar.
a: where the nectar is made: flower
who carries the nectar home: bee
where the nectar is dried: honeycomb
items.why: The flower makes nectar. A worker bee carries the nectar home. Bees dry the nectar in the honeycomb. Then it is honey.
items.art: Four boxes in a row joined by arrows: a flower, a bee flying, a honeycomb, a jar of honey, each with an empty label.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last.
items: Bees fan the nectar until it is thick.
A bee drinks the nectar and flies home.
a: A bee drinks the nectar and flies home.
Bees fan the nectar until it is thick.
items.why: Nectar is made first, then carried, then dried into honey, and last of all eaten.

items.p: Draw one food from a plant and one food from an animal that you ate today.
items.a: Any two true examples, such as a dosa and a glass of milk.
items.why: A strong drawing names both foods and can say who made each one.
items.art: An empty box split into two halves, one with a small leaf at the top and one with a small cow.

items.p: Think of the sugar water drop under the fan. What would it look like after two more days? Why?
items.a: Even smaller and harder, maybe a shiny crust. The moving air keeps taking water away until almost none is left.
items.why: A strong answer says what the child would see and says the water keeps leaving into the air.

items.p: A hen eats grain. A cow eats grass. Where did the food inside an egg and inside milk first come from?
items.a: From plants. The hen made the egg from the grain she ate, and the cow made the milk from the grass she ate.
items.why: Animals make milk and eggs from the food they eat, and that food was mostly plants.

items.p: Every food we eat comes from a plant or an animal.
items.why: False. Salt comes from sea water or from the ground, and no plant or animal makes water. A mushroom is a fungus, neither a plant nor an animal.

items.p: Sort these dishes: from plants only, from animals only, or both?
items.why: Plain rice is a seed. A boiled egg is from a hen. Curd rice and payasam mix rice with milk, so they are both.

items.p: Meera keeps honey bees in wooden boxes in Kodagu. Her friend Salma does not eat honey.

views.says: I take some honey and leave plenty for the bees. My bees also visit the coffee flowers, and that helps the coffee plants make more fruit.
The bees made the honey for their own hive. I would rather leave all of it for them.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one good reason the other one has.
items.a: A strong answer gives a reason for one side and a fair reason for the other: the beekeeper's bees help flowers make fruit, and the honey was made for the bees' own hive.
items.why: This is a real choice families make. Both sides care about the bees.

items.p: In the Be a Bee challenge, which tool carried the most sugar water? Draw that tool and its bottle cap.
items.a: A drawing of the best tool and a full cap.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the tool and how full its cap was, and the child can say why that tool held more.
items.art: An empty box with a bottle cap outline at the bottom.

items.p: Why do bees fan their wings over the honeycomb?
opts: To dry the nectar into honey
items.why: The moving air from their wings makes water evaporate from the nectar, until it is thick honey.

items.p: Match each food to the plant part we eat.
items.why: Rice grains are seeds. A mango is a fruit. Palak is a leaf. A carrot is a root.

items.p: Three of these are made from milk. Which one is not?
items.why: Ghee, paneer and curd are all made from milk. Jaggery is made from sugarcane juice, so jaggery comes from a plant.

items.p: Bees make honey from the sweet ____ inside flowers.
items.why: Nectar is the thin sweet juice that flowers make. Bees carry nectar home and dry it into honey.

items.p: Plants make their own food from sunlight. You cannot. So where does all your food come from?
items.a: From plants, from animals, and a little, like salt and water, from the Earth.
items.why: A strong answer says that people, like other animals, must eat food that plants or other animals made.

quiz.p: Which of these is food from an animal?
quiz.why: A cow, buffalo or goat makes milk. Idli is made from seeds, and a banana is a fruit.

quiz.p: Which of these is food from a plant?
quiz.why: A coconut is the fruit of the coconut palm. An egg comes from a hen, and curd is made from milk.

quiz.p: Which of these is neither from a plant nor from an animal?
quiz.why: Salt comes from sea water or from the ground. Rice is a seed, and ghee is made from milk.

quiz.p: How does a mango tree get food?
opts: The tree makes food in the leaves, from sunlight, air and water
quiz.why: Green plants make their own food in their leaves. The soil gives water and a little of some minerals, not food.

quiz.p: A goat eats leaves all day. Why does the goat need to eat?
opts: Goats, like all animals, get their food by eating
quiz.why: Animals, including goats and people, cannot make food from sunlight. So they eat plants, or other animals, or both.

quiz.p: What do honey bees make honey from?
quiz.why: Bees drink nectar from flowers, carry it home and dry it into honey.

quiz.p: In the sugar water test, why did we cover one drop with a katori?
opts: To see what happens when moving air cannot reach the drop
To keep ants off the drop
quiz.why: One drop was open and one was covered. Everything else was the same, so we could see what the moving air did.

quiz.p: Who makes the honey in a beehive?
quiz.why: The worker bees, who are all female, gather nectar and make honey. Male bees make no honey. The beekeeper only takes some out.

quiz.p: What does a cow eat to make her milk?
quiz.why: A cow makes milk from the grass, hay and other plants she eats.

quiz.p: Where does an egg come from?
quiz.why: A hen lays eggs. The shop only sells them.

quiz.p: Before you left the drops under the fan, what did you do first?
opts: Made a guess and said why
quiz.why: Scientists guess first and give a reason. Then the test shows if the guess was right.

applications: Beekeepers in Kodagu, Kerala and many other places keep honey bees in wooden boxes. The bees make honey and also carry pollen to coffee, coconut and fruit flowers.
India makes more milk than any other country. Most of it comes from cows and buffaloes kept by small farming families.
Farmers grow rice, wheat, ragi, dal and vegetables, which make up most of the food eaten in India.
Honey keeps for a very long time without spoiling, because it has so little water in it.

spotted.text: A huge rock bee comb hanging under a ledge or a water tank on a tall building, in Bengaluru, Hyderabad or Chennai. Watch from far away and never disturb it.

spotted.text: Green rice fields from a train window, in Thanjavur, Kerala, Bengal or Assam.

spotted.text: A fish market in Kochi or Kolkata, with fish just brought in from the sea or the river.

open_questions.q: How does a bee know which flowers still have nectar?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found that bees use colour and smell, and that bees leave scent marks on flowers they have emptied. How bees put all these clues together is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of bees live in India?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have named hundreds of kinds of bees in India, but many small wild bees have never been studied. Nobody has counted them all.
In 2016, scientists in London found that bumblebees given a sweet treat acted more hopeful about a new flower. Some scientists say this shows feelings. Others say it is too early to tell.

ask_kids: Which food on your plate came from a plant? Which came from an animal?
Who made the milk in your glass, and what did she eat?
If you were a bee, which flower would you visit first? Why?
Can you find a food at dinner that is from a plant and an animal at once?
What would you eat if you could make food from sunlight, like a plant?
Where do you think the rice in your house was grown?

jokes.a: Because they don't know the words!

jokes.j: What do you call a bee who can't make up her mind?
Which bee is good for your health?
What does a cow read every morning?
Where do cows go on a holiday?

jokes.a: Because they hang around in bunches!

jokes.j: What did the banana say to the doctor?
Why did the egg go to school?
What is a bee's favourite haircut?

maths.problem: Ammu sorted her lunch. She put 5 foods on the leaf plate and 2 foods on the cow plate. How many more foods are on the leaf plate?
maths.answer: 3 more foods are on the leaf plate.
maths.explain: Start at 2 and count on to 5: 3, 4, 5. That is 3 more. Most of her lunch came from plants.
maths.context: This is about Leaf Plate, Cow Plate, where you sort foods from plants and from animals. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Finding how many more shows at a glance which kind of food made up most of the lunch.

maths.problem: In a second go at the Be a Bee challenge, Sundari counted the dips each tool needed to fill a cap. The spoon needed 4 dips, the paintbrush 7 and the cotton bud 12. Put them in order, from the fewest dips to the most.
maths.explain: 4 is less than 7, and 7 is less than 12. The fewer dips a tool needs, the more it carries each time. So the spoon carried most each dip, and the cotton bud least.
maths.context: This is about the Be a Bee challenge, where tools carry sugar water like a bee's tongue. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Putting the numbers in order tells us which tool works best, and fewer dips means more carried each time.

maths.problem: Zoya's food week had 30 green dots and 6 red dots. Her cousin Bindu, who eats fish every day, had 24 green dots and 14 red dots. Who ate more food from animals? Who ate more food from plants?
maths.answer: Bindu had more red dots, so she ate more food from animals. Zoya had more green dots, so she ate more food from plants.
maths.explain: 14 is more than 6, so Bindu had more red dots. 30 is more than 24, so Zoya had more green dots. Both girls still had more green dots than red dots.
maths.context: This is about the food week project, where you put a green dot for each plant food and a red dot for each animal food. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two sets of dots shows how two families eat differently, and what is the same for both.

founder: ideas/by_topic/food-and-a-balanced-diet.md: the SCI cards there (Barry Marshall, M. S. Swaminathan) suit higher levels and were not used at Level 1. Its oneness line, that the food on a plate was sunlight, soil, rain, bees and someone's work, shaped the honey thread.
science: Aristotle, History of Animals, Book 5: honey described as falling from the air and gathered by bees.
Charles Butler (1609). The Feminine Monarchie. Luis Méndez de Torres (1586) first wrote that the large bee is a female who lays eggs.
Jan Swammerdam's dissections of the queen bee, 1669 to the 1670s, published in Biblia Naturae (1737 to 1738).

roots.context: We have sorted foods from plants and foods from animals, and turned thin sugar water thick. Now we ask what honey tells us about how plants, animals and we are joined.

deep_truth.truth: Our thin sugar water, left under the fan, turned thick and sticky like honey. The moving air took its water away. Bees thicken flower nectar the same way, by fanning it. A flower made the nectar and bees made the honey, so honey needs a plant and an animal.
deep_truth.habit: We sort every food into two boxes, plant or animal, as if each food has one maker. Honey needs both: a flower made the nectar, and bees changed it into honey.
deep_truth.evidence: In the sugar water test, the open drop under the fan turned thick and barely moved when tilted, while the covered drop stayed runny. Bees dry nectar in the comb by fanning it with their wings.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal too. Like every animal, you must eat what plants and other animals made.
three.what_is_life: Life passes food along. A flower makes nectar, a bee makes honey, and you eat the honey.
three.what_is_this_world: A world where flowers and bees feed each other. The bee gets nectar, and the flower gets pollen carried to the next flower.

roots.thread: Sunlight falls on a leaf, and the plant makes sugar. The flower turns some of that sugar into nectar. A bee drinks the nectar, and bees dry the nectar into honey, and you eat the honey. The same sunlight has become a plant's food, a bee's food and your food.

teachings.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.5.1 (the Madhu Vidya, the teaching of honey)
teachings.teaching: This earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth.
teachings.link: In honey, a flower feeds the bees and the bees help the flower make seeds. Each one is food and help for the other, as the teaching says.

teachings.teaching: A bee gathers nectar from a flower without harming the flower's colour or smell, and flies away. A wise person moves through the village in the same way.
teachings.link: A bee takes nectar but leaves the flower whole, and carries the flower's pollen on. Taking food does not have to mean harming.

science.text: Many fruits and vegetables grow only when bees and other insects carry pollen between their flowers.
A honey bee dances on the comb to tell her sisters which way the flowers are, and how far.

other_view.view: They say bees and flowers do not mean to help each other. Each one does what helps their own life, and the help to the other happens along the way.

practice.title: One Slow Drop
practice.say: Put one drop of honey, or a crumb of jaggery, on your tongue. Close your eyes. Let it melt slowly. Think of the flower that made the sweet juice. Think of the bee, or the sugarcane field. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly, three times. Now open your eyes.
practice.kid: Put one drop of honey on your tongue. Close your eyes. Let it melt. Think of the flower. Breathe in and out, three times. Open your eyes.

ask: If honey is from a flower and from bees, are there other foods that came from more than one living being?
The bees made the honey for their own hive. What do you think the bees would say about us eating it?
A plant makes food from sunlight, and you eat the plant. Is some of that sunlight now inside you?
roots.art: A child with eyes closed and a drop of honey on a spoon, with a faint flower and a bee drawn above them.

how_we_found_out.context: Who makes the honey in a hive? This card tells the true story of how people found out.
how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time, people in Europe believed that a king bee ruled every hive. The Greek thinker Aristotle wrote about the king bee about 2,350 years ago. He also wrote that honey falls from the air, and the bees only gather it. Beekeepers watched their bees closely, and saw them drinking from flowers. In 1586, a Spanish beekeeper named Luis Méndez de Torres wrote that the big bee in the hive is a female who lays eggs. In 1609, the English beekeeper Charles Butler said the same in a book called The Feminine Monarchie. Many people still did not believe it. Then, around 350 years ago, the Dutch scientist Jan Swammerdam cut open the big bee and looked inside with a microscope. He found the parts that make eggs. The king was a queen, the mother of the whole hive. Today we know more. The queen lays the eggs. The worker bees, who are all female too, gather nectar and make the honey. The male bees make no honey at all.
how_we_found_out.who: Luis Méndez de Torres, Charles Butler and Jan Swammerdam
how_we_found_out.when: 1586, 1609, and Swammerdam's dissections between 1669 and the 1670s
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a male king bee rules the hive, and that honey falls from the air. Swammerdam's microscope showed the big bee makes eggs, so she is a mother, and watching bees showed honey is made from flower nectar.
how_we_found_out.art: An old wooden table with a microscope, a large bee on a glass slide, and a drawing of a honeycomb beside it.

playtest: Walked through the sugar water test, the lunch sort, the feely bag, the ants' menu, the food week, both games and the bee tongue challenge as a parent and a six-year-old in a city flat would. Fixed: the sorting game scored two ways (cards kept versus cards left on plates), so wrong guesses now move the card and right guesses earn a mark; the bee challenge listed five tools but said four caps and four tools; the feely bag could have no animal food, so paneer is the swap for families without eggs; the sugar water step said to leave plates until morning but the evening look came first; 'was never alive' lines for salt and water now say what is true without denying anything; the story note lost its internal wording; video titles lost their working notes; the food week question no longer assumes sambar; and repeated sugar water questions in the sheets and quiz were replaced with new ones. The sugar water test needs only sugar, water, two steel plates, a katori and a fan, and is checked the next morning. Both games have every card written out.
